actions.action: Deploy automated multi-touchpoint SMS/email notifications for all service and parts interactions, triggered at four mandatory milestones: (1) vehicle checked in, (2) technician diagnosis complete with quoted cost, (3) work approved and in progress, (4) vehicle ready for collection. Configure via the DMS (e.g. Pentana/Reynolds) at all 24 sites, with VIC01 Dandenong, QLD01 Chermside, and NSW02 Penrith prioritised for rollout in Week 1 given their volume (65, 57, and 53 complaints respectively). For parts orders specifically, add a fifth automated trigger when a back-order ETA is confirmed or changes. Customers should also be offered channel preference (SMS, email, or both) at booking to address the accessibility gap evidenced by at least one customer who is deaf and was only contacted by phone.
actions.owner: Service Operations Manager (national) + IT/DMS Administrator, with Site Service Managers accountable for local activation and staff compliance
actions.measure: Primary: Reduce 'No updates / had to chase' complaints (currently 389, the single largest sub-theme at 45.5% of total) by at least 50% within two service review cycles (approx. 3 months). Secondary: Track outbound-to-inbound contact ratio in DMS call logs — target shift so dealership-initiated contacts exceed customer-initiated contacts. Tertiary: Post-service NPS/CSI survey question on proactive communication scores above 7/10 for 80% of respondents.
actions.rationale: At 389 incidents, 'No updates / had to chase' is the dominant sub-theme, dwarfing all others. The sample comments show an overwhelming pattern: customers across Service (556 cases), Parts (71), and Sales (56) are universally describing the same failure — zero proactive outreach, with every update requiring customer-initiated contact. This is a structural process gap, not a people skills gap. Automation removes human dependency from the update loop entirely and addresses the problem at scale across all 24 sites simultaneously. The trend is Stable (not improving), meaning no organic fix is occurring; systemic intervention is required. Only 4 complaints are tagged 'Proactive updates' (positive), suggesting almost no sites have this working at present.

actions.action: Implement a mandatory callback management system to eliminate the 'message black hole' pattern. Specifically: (a) Replace informal paper/verbal message-taking with a DMS-logged callback task assigned directly to the named staff member, with a 2-hour SLA for return. (b) If the assigned staff member does not action within 2 hours, the task auto-escalates to their team leader or Service Manager. (c) All front desk staff at Customer Service/Front Desk to be retrained within 30 days on the new protocol — training to include role-play scenarios reflecting the exact failure mode seen in comments (message taken at front desk, never passed to tech or advisor). (d) Introduce a daily end-of-day callback audit: Service Managers at each site to review any open/unresolved callback tasks before close of business. Prioritise QLD08 Townsville and NSW01 Parramatta for immediate audit given their complaint volumes (49 and 48) and the 'Callback not returned' sub-theme representing 282 cases (33% of total).
actions.owner: Customer Service/Front Desk Team Leaders (site level) + Service Managers, overseen by State Operations Managers
actions.measure: Primary: Reduce 'Callback not returned' complaints (currently 282) by 60% within 90 days. Secondary: Reduce 'Message not passed on' sub-theme (currently 107 cases) by 70% within 90 days — this sub-theme is the clearest indicator of internal relay failure specifically. Tertiary: DMS callback task completion rate should reach 95%+ within SLA window within 60 days of rollout.
actions.rationale: The 'Callback not returned' (282) and 'Message not passed on' (107) sub-themes together account for 389 cases — nearly identical in scale to 'No updates / had to chase'. However, these represent a distinct and compounding failure: customers who actively tried to reach the business and were still ignored. Comments name specific staff (Sarah, Raj, Josh, Ben, Aroha, Linh, Tuan) and describe an internal relay system that is broken — messages taken at front desk consistently fail to reach mechanics, advisors, or parts staff. This is a workflow and accountability failure. The Customer Service/Front Desk department (153 cases) is the structural chokepoint. Note: some individual staff names appear repeatedly across complaints (Sarah, Raj, Ben, Josh), which may indicate specific coaching needs at site level — however, the data does not confirm site attribution for named individuals with certainty, so this is flagged as a hypothesis for Site Managers to investigate via 1:1 review rather than group action.

actions.action: Conduct an urgent phone infrastructure and call-handling audit at the five highest-complaint dealerships (VIC01, QLD01, NSW02, QLD08, NSW01), with specific focus on: (a) average hold times and abandoned call rates — target maximum 3-minute hold time and below 5% call abandonment; (b) voicemail box monitoring — establish whether general service voicemail boxes are being checked and by whom, with a named responsible owner per site; (c) website enquiry form and email triage — audit current response times for online form submissions and emails (multiple comments describe triple-channel outreach with zero response); (d) based on audit findings, implement minimum staffing standards for phone coverage during peak hours (noted as a particular issue in comments referencing 10–20+ minute holds). Findings to be reported to State Operations Managers within 45 days with a remediation plan per site.
actions.owner: State Operations Managers (audit and accountability) + Site Service Managers + IT/Telephony team (infrastructure)
actions.measure: Primary: Reduce 'Phone unanswered / long hold' complaints (currently 69) by 50% within 60 days of remediation implementation. Secondary: Average hold time as measured by telephony system logs to fall below 3 minutes across all five audited sites. Tertiary: Online enquiry response time to be brought to within 4 business hours, measured via CRM ticket timestamps.
actions.rationale: While 'Phone unanswered / long hold' (69 cases) is the smallest quantified sub-theme, it is a compounding failure — customers who cannot get through on the phone cannot even begin the callback process, and several comments describe abandoning digital channels (email, web forms) with equal futility. This represents a channel access problem that amplifies all other communication failures. The five highest-volume dealerships are the logical starting point. This is ranked third because automation (Action 1) and callback process reform (Action 2) will together address the majority of volume; phone infrastructure is a necessary but supporting fix. Caution: the audit may reveal that hold times are partly a staffing/resourcing issue rather than a technology one — budget implications should be flagged to senior leadership if that is the finding.

actions.action: Implement a mandatory written pre-authorisation workflow for all service work: (1) Provide customers with a fully itemised written quote before any work begins, including all consumables, sundry fees, environmental levies, fluid top-ups, and labour hours with book-time justification. (2) Require explicit customer sign-off (digital or physical) before any additional work beyond the original quote is commenced — no exceptions. (3) Where additional work is identified mid-service, the Service Advisor must phone the customer, obtain verbal approval, record it on the job card with timestamp, and follow up with an SMS confirmation of the revised total. (4) Configure the DMS to block invoice generation if uninitiated line items appear without a corresponding approval record.
actions.owner: Service Manager (all sites, led by State Service Directors) with DMS/IT support for system configuration
actions.measure: Primary: Reduce 'Unexpected/unauthorised charges' complaints (currently 184, the single largest sub-theme at 50% of all issues) by 50% within two service quarters. Secondary: Track the percentage of invoices that match the original written quote within a 5% tolerance — target 90%+ match rate within 90 days. Monitor via monthly DMS invoice-vs-quote variance report by site, with VIC02 Ringwood, QLD01 Chermside, and NSW01 Parramatta as highest-priority sites given their complaint volumes (28, 27, and 27 respectively).
actions.rationale: Unexpected/unauthorised charges (184 issues) and quote-exceeded-without-notice (102 issues) together account for 286 of 367 complaints — 78% of this theme. The feedback is unambiguous: customers are being charged for work they did not approve, including fuel system cleans, cabin filters, tyre rotations, wiper blades, fluid flushes, and a range of vaguely labelled sundry fees, with no prior call or written notification. This is not a pricing perception problem — it is a consent and process failure. Several comments describe customers paying under duress (pensioners, students, parents with small children) because they felt unable to challenge the bill at the counter. The 250 'High' severity ratings and 2 'Critical' ratings confirm the financial and trust impact is significant. This action addresses the root cause directly and will have the broadest impact across all affected sites and departments.

actions.action: Conduct an urgent invoice accuracy audit across all 24 sites, then implement a permanent invoice quality-check gate: (1) Within 30 days, pull the last 90 days of invoices from the top five affected sites (VIC02, QLD01, NSW01, QLD08, VIC06) and cross-reference each against the original written quote — flag all variances, duplicate line items, and unapproved additions. Identify and remediate any systemic billing errors (e.g. 5 tyre valves on a 4-wheel vehicle, double-charged oil filters, coolant top-up billed as a full flush, labour hours exceeding book time without justification). (2) Issue credits proactively to affected customers identified in the audit — do not wait for them to complain. (3) Going forward, require a second-check sign-off by the Service Manager or nominated deputy on any invoice that exceeds the original quote by more than $50 or 10%, whichever is lower, before it is presented to the customer.
actions.owner: Service Manager (audit and ongoing gate) supported by Finance/Business Office (billing reconciliation) and State Operations Managers (oversight)
actions.measure: Invoice discrepancy complaints (currently 75) to reduce by 60% within two quarters. Track: number of proactive credits issued in audit phase; percentage of invoices failing the second-check gate; repeat invoice dispute rate per site. Report monthly to State Operations Managers. Hypothesis to validate during audit: the pattern of specific recurring erroneous line items (5 tyre valves, duplicate labour, coolant top-up vs flush, labour hours above book time) may indicate a small number of individual advisors or a DMS default-billing issue rather than a site-wide culture problem — the audit data will clarify this.
actions.rationale: Invoice discrepancy complaints (75 issues) represent a distinct sub-problem from unauthorised charges — these are cases where the arithmetic, line items, or product specifications on the invoice are factually wrong (double-charged parts, incorrect quantities, wrong product billed). Multiple customers specifically flagged they only caught errors by checking on their phone or calculator in the car park, or by reading the invoice at home. Several vulnerable customers — pensioners, new car owners, those with young children — describe paying without scrutinising because they were in a stressful environment. A proactive audit and credit programme will recover trust more effectively than waiting for disputes, and the invoice gate will prevent recurrence. Finance/Business Office is implicated in 71 of 367 complaints, suggesting the problem extends beyond the service lane into finance and sales contracting as well.

actions.action: Standardise and publish a transparent fee schedule for all common ancillary charges across the dealership group, and train all customer-facing staff to disclose and explain these fees at the time of booking — not at invoice. Specifically: (1) Identify all recurring sundry and ancillary charges currently appearing on invoices (consumables, shop supplies, environmental levy, fuel surcharge, handling, admin, diagnostic, battery health check, etc.) and make a group-level decision: either absorb these into the base labour rate, or formally price and name them consistently. (2) Publish the agreed fee schedule on the website, the booking app, and the printed service menu at reception. (3) Update booking confirmation emails and SMS to include a plain-English statement: 'Your quoted price covers [X]. Additional charges that may apply include [Y] — we will always contact you before adding anything.' (4) Deliver a 30-minute briefing to all Service Advisors at the top five sites on how to explain ancillary fees in simple terms at drop-off, not at pick-up.
actions.owner: National Service Operations Manager (fee schedule decision and publishing) and Customer Experience / Marketing (website, app, comms) with Site Service Managers owning staff training delivery
actions.measure: Reduction in complaints specifically referencing named ancillary fees ('consumables', 'shop supplies', 'environmental levy', 'fuel surcharge', 'admin fee', etc.) — currently estimated at 40–60 of the 184 unauthorised charge complaints based on comment patterns. Target: 70% reduction in these specific line-item complaints within two quarters. Track via complaint categorisation in CRM. Secondary measure: customer satisfaction score on 'price transparency' in the post-service survey. Note: this action is lower priority than Actions 1 and 2 because it addresses perception and communication of legitimate fees, whereas Actions 1 and 2 address the more serious problem of charges being added without consent or containing factual errors. The trend being stable (not declining) suggests no current intervention is working, and the group has not yet addressed root causes.
actions.rationale: A recurring pattern across the feedback is customers being blindsided by small, vaguely named fees — 'shop sundries', 'consumables', 'environmental levy', 'fuel surcharge', 'admin fee', 'vehicle handover fee' — that appear nowhere on the quote and are not explained at drop-off. Several technically sophisticated customers noted these are being used to pad totals (e.g. one customer calculated shop sundries at 8% of labour). Whether these fees are legitimate or not, the current practice of disclosing them only at invoice is fuelling distrust and complaints. Standardising and publishing the fee schedule removes the perception of a 'hidden fee' model and reduces counter confrontations. The trend being stable across H1 and H2 confirms this is a structural issue, not a seasonal or one-off problem, and will not self-correct without deliberate intervention.

actions.action: Implement a mandatory pre-service parts availability check for all booked jobs, at least 48 hours prior to the customer's appointment. Service Advisors must confirm all required parts are on-site before the booking is confirmed. Where parts are unavailable, customers must be proactively contacted to reschedule or offered a loan vehicle. Simultaneously, enforce a real-time job-status board visible to all service desk staff so every advisor can see live vehicle progress and communicate accurate pickup ETAs without the customer needing to chase.
actions.owner: Service Manager (each site) with Group Parts & Service Director overseeing rollout — prioritise NSW01 Parramatta, VIC01 Dandenong, and QLD01 Chermside as the three highest-volume offenders
actions.measure: Reduce 'Vehicle not ready when promised' complaints (currently 101 issues, second-largest sub-theme) by 50% within two service quarters. Track via post-visit survey question: 'Was your vehicle ready at the time promised?' Target: 85% yes-rate within 6 months. Also track parts-not-available-on-day incidents as a separate operational KPI, reported monthly per site.
actions.rationale: Parts unavailability is a recurring and highly disruptive driver of broken promise times — multiple comments describe customers losing full work days, school pickups, and shifts because a bearing, gasket kit, sensor, or control arm bush wasn't in stock and nobody told them in advance. This compounds into the 'Vehicle not ready when promised' sub-theme (101 issues) and 'Long service turnaround' (122 issues), which together account for over half of all complaints. The impact is severe for customers with dependants, shift workers, fleet operators, and students — groups explicitly represented in the feedback. At 68 High-severity issues group-wide, this is the fastest route to reducing the most damaging complaints. The trend is stable (not improving), indicating no spontaneous resolution is occurring.

actions.action: Restructure service desk staffing and queuing at the five highest-affected sites (NSW01, VIC01, QLD01, VIC03, QLD08) to ensure a minimum of two staff on the service reception counter during peak periods (7:30–9:30am drop-off and 2:00–5:00pm pickup). Introduce a dedicated express lane for key drop-off and key collection only, separate from the full service advisor queue. Queue wait time at drop-off and collection must not exceed 10 minutes. Where full resourcing is not immediately viable, implement a numbered ticket or SMS queue system so customers are not physically standing in line.
actions.owner: Service Manager at each affected site, with HR/Workforce Planning supporting roster changes — Group Operations Manager to set the 10-minute queue standard as a non-negotiable KPI
actions.measure: Reduce 'Queue / desk wait' complaints (currently 111 issues, largest single sub-theme) by 40% within two quarters. Measure via: (1) post-visit survey question 'How long did you wait at the counter on arrival and collection?' with target median under 10 minutes; (2) mystery shop at each of the five priority sites once per quarter to observe peak-hour desk staffing levels. Review staff roster data monthly against complaint volume per site.
actions.rationale: Queue and desk wait is the single largest sub-theme at 111 issues and the pattern in the comments is unambiguous: one staff member serving a line of 10–15 customers, 25–50 minute waits just to hand over or collect keys, and in several cases customers with young children, elderly customers, and non-English-speaking customers bearing the worst of it. Multiple comments name specific staff (Tuan, Kylie, Mick) as the sole person working the desk — this is a structural resourcing problem, not a people problem. The 91 front desk/customer service issues confirm this extends beyond the workshop. NSW01 and VIC01 dominate the volume, suggesting these sites may have the most acute staffing gaps. This action will have visible, immediate impact on customer perception because the queue is often the first and last touchpoint of every visit.

actions.action: Standardise and enforce realistic service time quoting across all 24 dealerships by introducing a labour time guide cross-referenced with current technician capacity at the time of booking. Service Advisors must not quote turnaround times that assume zero queue or full technician availability. Where a job is estimated to take more than 3 hours, customers must be offered a courtesy vehicle or shuttle service at the time of booking, not after arrival. Introduce a 'promise time' field in the DMS that triggers an automatic outbound SMS or call to the customer 60 minutes before that time if the job is not yet complete — giving the customer advance warning rather than a surprise at the counter.
actions.owner: Service Advisors (quoting accountability) and Service Manager (enforcing labour time standards) — Group IT/DMS Administrator to configure the promise-time alert trigger in the dealer management system
actions.measure: Reduce 'Long service turnaround' complaints (currently 122 issues, the largest sub-theme) by 30% within three quarters, measured via post-visit survey. Track the gap between quoted and actual completion time per job as a monthly operational metric per site, with a target that 90% of jobs are completed within 30 minutes of the quoted time. Courtesy vehicle utilisation rate to be reported monthly as a proxy for whether longer-job customers are being accommodated proactively.
actions.rationale: A large portion of the frustration in the feedback is not just that waits are long — it is that the quoted time bears no resemblance to reality. Customers are repeatedly told '45 minutes', '2 hours', or 'ready by lunch' and then wait 4–6 hours, missing work shifts, school pickups, university classes, and medical appointments. This is a quoting accuracy problem as much as a throughput problem. Notably, several comments acknowledge that SMS updates were appreciated (a positive signal that proactive communication works), but the updates simply confirmed ongoing delays rather than preventing them. This action builds on what is already working (digital communication) while addressing the root cause of unrealistic promises. This is ranked third because solving parts availability (Action 1) and desk resourcing (Action 2) will reduce some of the turnaround blowouts organically — but inaccurate quoting is a separate systemic issue that requires its own fix. Hypothesis: sites like NSW01 and VIC01 may be systematically under-quoting to win bookings; this warrants a targeted audit of quoted vs actual times at those sites specifically.

actions.action: Launch a mandatory 'Frontline Behaviours' reset program at the five highest-volume sites (QLD01 Chermside, NSW02 Penrith, VIC01 Dandenong, VIC02 Ringwood, QLD04 Southport), targeting Service Advisors and Customer Service/Front Desk staff first. The program must be grounded in observed failure modes from feedback: (a) dismissing or talking over customers who self-identify as inexperienced or non-English-speaking, (b) non-verbal rudeness (eye-rolls, sighs, avoiding eye contact, walking away mid-sentence), and (c) responding to legitimate complaints with deflection ('it's on the invoice', 'not my department'). Delivery format: 3-hour in-dealership workshop per site within 60 days, facilitated by an external customer experience trainer using anonymised verbatim feedback from this dataset as case material. Reinforce with a 10-point Service Interaction Standard posted at each service and front desk station, covering greet, acknowledge, explain, and close. Named repeat offenders identified in feedback (Jess, Kylie, Bec, Josh, Tuan, Mick, Gaz across multiple comments) should be managed via individual performance conversations by their direct manager within 30 days, separate from the group program.
actions.owner: General Manager – each affected site, supported by Group HR and an external CX training provider
actions.measure: Primary: reduction in 'Rude/dismissive/unhelpful' sub-theme complaints from 163 (current H2 baseline) by at least 30% within two post-training quarters, tracked via the same feedback categorisation system. Secondary: post-interaction CSI scores for Service and Front Desk at the five target sites, benchmarked against current site averages. Tertiary: reduction in staff named negatively in feedback (currently 38 instances) by 50% within 12 months.
actions.rationale: 'Rude/dismissive/unhelpful' accounts for 163 of 221 issues (74%) and 117 of 221 are rated High severity — the dominant and most damaging sub-theme by a wide margin. Service (91 issues) and Customer Service/Front Desk (54 issues) together represent 65% of all department mentions. The five named sites account for 86 complaints between them. The feedback strongly and consistently shows a pattern of staff dismissing customers who are inexperienced, non-English-speaking, younger, lower-income, or new to the area — a vulnerability cluster that amplifies reputational and retention risk. Multiple named staff members appear across more than one comment, suggesting individual behaviour problems that group training alone will not resolve. The trend is stable (not improving), meaning no self-correction is occurring and intervention is required.

actions.action: Implement a group-wide 'Finance & Sales Pressure' protocol to eliminate high-pressure add-on selling across all 24 dealerships, with immediate focus on Finance/Business Office and Sales departments. The protocol must include: (a) a single-decline rule — if a customer declines an add-on product (paint protection, extended warranty, gap cover, finance) once, the staff member is not permitted to re-raise it in the same interaction; (b) a written 'take-home review' offer for all finance and insurance products, with customers explicitly told they have 48 hours to review before committing; (c) removal of any same-day urgency language ('this offer is only available today') from approved scripts and verbal practice. Train all Sales and Finance staff on the updated protocol within 45 days. Flag this as a compliance and consumer law risk to the Board: several comments describe conduct consistent with pressure selling and potential Australian Consumer Law concerns (e.g., misrepresenting that finance with the dealership is required to obtain the advertised price, and continuing to push products after repeated refusals).
actions.owner: National Sales Director and Group Finance/Business Manager, with Legal/Compliance review
actions.measure: Reduction in 'Pressuring/pushy' sub-theme complaints from 20 to fewer than 5 within two quarters post-implementation. Monthly mystery shopping at a minimum of 6 sites (rotating) to audit compliance with the single-decline rule and take-home offer. Zero recurrence of comments referencing 'only available today' or 'you have no choice on finance' language within 6 months. Note: 20 complaints is a relatively small count, but the severity of individual cases (customers feeling coerced, not understanding what they signed, being told pricing changes without dealer finance) elevates this to a legal and reputational risk that warrants priority treatment disproportionate to its volume.
actions.rationale: Although 'Pressuring/pushy' is the smallest sub-theme at 20 complaints, the qualitative content is serious: multiple customers describe feeling unable to leave without agreeing to something, not understanding contracts they signed under pressure, and being told the advertised price was conditional on taking dealer finance. These patterns carry potential Australian Consumer Law exposure under unfair contract terms and unconscionable conduct provisions. The Finance/Business Office (5 issues) and Sales (47 issues) are both implicated. This is prioritised above the named-staff action because the risk profile extends beyond customer satisfaction into regulatory territory.

actions.action: Establish a structured 'Vulnerable and Inexperienced Customer' awareness standard across all customer-facing roles, embedded into onboarding for new staff and annual refreshers for existing staff. The standard should define recognition cues (customer states they are new to cars, new to the area, a first-time buyer, have language difficulties, or are managing dependants during the visit) and prescribe specific minimum responses: slow down, avoid jargon, offer written summaries, proactively ask if they need anything repeated, and never laugh at, sigh at, or talk over a customer who asks a basic question. Pair this with a 'First Experience' checklist for Service Advisors to use at vehicle drop-off for customers who identify as first-timers, covering: what will happen today, when you will hear from us, who to call, and what the likely cost range is. This directly addresses a pattern that appears across Parts, Service, and Sales feedback.
actions.owner: Group Training & Development Manager, implemented via Dealership Principals at all 24 sites
actions.measure: Reduction in feedback comments referencing customers feeling 'talked down to', 'made to feel stupid', 'dismissed for not knowing terminology', or similar language — currently identifiable in approximately 40-50 comments in this dataset. Measure via qualitative tagging in the feedback system at each six-month review. Additionally, track whether complaints from customers who self-identify as new to the area, first-time buyers, or non-English-speaking decline as a proportion of total feedback within 12 months. Note: the data does not allow us to quantify this sub-group precisely, so the 40-50 figure is a hypothesis based on manual reading of the sample — the feedback system should be updated to tag this vulnerability cluster explicitly going forward.
actions.rationale: A clearly recurring pattern across the 200-comment sample is staff behaving dismissively or impatiently specifically toward customers who are inexperienced, new to the area, non-English-speaking, students, or managing children. This is not random rudeness — it is directional, targeting customers with less confidence or leverage, which is both an ethical problem and a retention risk (these customers, once lost, rarely return). The issue spans Service, Parts, Sales, and Front Desk, making it a cross-functional cultural gap rather than a site-specific one. Addressing it through a defined standard is lower-lift than the full behavioural reset program (Priority 1) but complements it by giving staff concrete, observable behaviours rather than abstract expectations.

actions.action: Implement a mandatory pre-delivery test protocol requiring the attending technician AND a second-check advisor to verify the original fault is resolved before the vehicle is returned to the customer. Specifically: (1) the job card must include a 'fault verification' field completed by the tech with a road-test or functional-test result; (2) a service advisor must countersign the job card confirming the original fault description has been addressed; (3) where the fault cannot be reproduced or resolved, the customer must be called before pickup is offered — not after collection. This protocol must be trained and rolled out across all 24 sites within 60 days, with QLD01 (Chermside), VIC03 (Essendon), VIC02 (Ringwood), NSW01 (Parramatta), and VIC05 (Box Hill) prioritised in weeks 1–3 given their disproportionate complaint volumes.
actions.owner: National Service Operations Manager, with site-level accountability held by each dealership's Service Manager
actions.measure: Primary KPI: reduce 'issue not resolved / recurring fault' complaints (currently 244 of 377 issues, 65% of theme) by 40% within two service quarters. Secondary KPIs: first-visit fix rate tracked monthly per site via DMS job card data; re-visit rate for same fault within 30 days reported in weekly service dashboard. Note: current data does not tell us whether faults are failing due to misdiagnosis, inadequate parts, or rushed labour — hypothesis is it is a mix of all three, so the dual sign-off protocol targets the output regardless of root cause, while management investigates root cause per site.
actions.rationale: This is the single largest sub-theme at 244 complaints (65% of all Repair & Service Quality issues) and carries the highest severity weighting — the majority of the 261 High and 25 Critical flags relate to recurring faults (e.g. oil leaks back within days, ABS lights returning same evening, brake repairs failing immediately, safety-critical items such as loose wheel nuts, unsecured bonnets, and loose battery terminals). The trend is stable, meaning no natural improvement is occurring. Recurring faults also drive compounding costs: customers are returning multiple times, losing income, and losing trust. The five highest-volume sites each register 26–28 complaints, suggesting this is a systemic process failure rather than isolated individual performance.

actions.action: Introduce a standardised vehicle presentation checklist completed by the technician at job completion and verified by the wash-bay or delivery coordinator before every customer handover. The checklist must include: wipe-down of all touched surfaces (steering wheel, door panels, seat, seatbelt, gear knob, roof lining, pedals); confirmation that all loose items (caps, clips, bolts, hubcaps, filter covers, rags, tools) are removed from the vehicle; a walkaround inspection for new bodywork damage (scratches, dents, paint chips) signed off against a pre-drop-off condition report; and confirmation that all consumables disturbed during the service (oil caps, coolant caps, air filter covers, wheel nuts) are properly secured. Where a wash service is offered, establish a strict protocol that muddy vehicles are vacuumed before washing, not after. Roll this out with a laminated checklist physically attached to each job card.
actions.owner: Service Manager at each site, with the wash-bay lead or delivery coordinator as day-to-day process owner
actions.measure: Reduce 'vehicle returned dirty or damaged' complaints (currently 86 of 377, 23% of theme) by 50% within two service quarters. Track via: monthly complaint coding in CRM; a 'vehicle presentation' score added to the post-service customer satisfaction survey (single question, 1–5); and a damage claim register reviewed by each Service Manager weekly. Hypothesis: the damage complaints (scratches, dents) may partly reflect pre-existing damage being disputed — pre-drop-off condition photography (timestamped, stored in DMS) would reduce disputed claims and is recommended as a complementary measure, though this data alone cannot confirm whether damage is dealership-caused or pre-existing in all cases.
actions.rationale: 86 complaints about vehicles returned dirty or physically damaged represent 23% of this theme and appear across all five high-volume sites. The comments reveal a consistent pattern of greasy handprints on steering wheels, door panels, roof linings, seat belts, and cream upholstery; mud transferred inside cabs; tools and rags left in engine bays; and new scratches and dents on bodywork. Several comments describe safety-adjacent issues (grease on pedals causing slipping, open bonnets). This sub-theme is entirely preventable with a checklist and accountability step — it does not require diagnostic skill, only process discipline — making it high-impact relative to implementation effort.

actions.action: Establish a formal internal communication protocol for job-specific customer messages between service advisors and technicians. Specifically: (1) any fault description, additional noise, or customer concern raised at drop-off must be entered as a line item on the digital job card in the DMS — verbal relay to technicians is to be discontinued as a primary method; (2) where a customer leaves a phone or voicemail message during the service period about their vehicle, the service advisor must log it in the DMS against the job and confirm with the customer within two business hours that it has been received; (3) all technician-to-advisor updates on parts availability, delays, or unresolved faults must be logged in the DMS and communicated to the customer same-day — not held until pickup. Conduct a one-day workshop at each of the five highest-volume sites within 90 days, using real examples from the complaints data to illustrate the failure mode.
actions.owner: Service Manager (process design and enforcement); Service Advisors (day-to-day execution); DMS/IT Administrator (job card configuration)
actions.measure: Reduce complaints referencing internal communication breakdowns — messages not passed on, no callbacks, customers having to chase — by 40% within two service quarters. Track via: a dedicated complaint sub-code 'internal communication failure' in the CRM; callback compliance rate audited monthly (sample of 20 jobs per site where customer left a message during service); and inclusion of a 'were your concerns communicated to the technician?' question in the post-service survey. Note: this action addresses the 'sloppy workmanship' and 'recurring fault' sub-themes only indirectly — it will not fix poor technical outcomes on its own, but the data shows a clear secondary pattern where correct fault information never reached the technician in the first place, meaning some 'unresolved fault' complaints may actually be communication failures rather than workmanship failures.
actions.rationale: Multiple comments across the dataset explicitly describe faults not being communicated from advisor to technician: customers who left detailed messages at drop-off found the mechanic had never been told; voicemails to named staff members went unreturned; customers had to call three or four times with no response; and in one case a customer had to re-explain their entire fault history from scratch on a second call because no record existed. This pattern appears across sites and vehicle types, suggesting a structural gap in how job information flows internally rather than isolated advisor negligence. While this sub-issue is lower in raw complaint volume than the other two actions, it likely inflates both the 'recurring fault' and 'sloppy workmanship' counts — resolving it could have a multiplier effect on the primary action's outcomes.

actions.action: Introduce a mandatory pre-handover Safety Sign-Off Checklist — a physical or digital form that must be completed and co-signed by the technician and a supervising service advisor before any vehicle is returned to a customer. The checklist must include as minimum: all wheel nuts torqued to spec and recorded, bonnet and all access panels latched, oil and coolant caps secured, brake pedal firmness check, tyre pressure confirmed and TPMS reset, no fluids visible on engine bay surfaces, no loose tools or foreign objects left in engine bay or boot, and all reported fault codes or symptoms re-tested via a short road test. Vehicles failing any item must be held until corrected. The form must be scanned to the job file. Priority implementation at VIC01 (Dandenong), NSW01 (Parramatta) and VIC05 (Box Hill) given their combined 33 issues — the three highest-volume sites.
actions.owner: Service Manager (each site), with Group Service Operations Manager accountable for rollout and compliance auditing
actions.measure: (1) Zero recurrence of loose wheel nut, unsecured bonnet, or loose oil/coolant cap complaints within 90 days of rollout — these three sub-issues account for at least 20+ clearly preventable incidents in the sample. (2) Monthly audit of completed checklists vs. job cards — target 100% completion rate within 60 days. (3) Reduction in Safety-themed complaints at VIC01, NSW01, and VIC05 by at least 50% in the subsequent half-year period.
actions.rationale: All 131 issues are rated Critical — the highest possible severity — and the trend is stable, meaning no improvement is occurring without intervention. The most alarming sub-patterns are finish-line failures: wheel nuts left loose (12 dedicated sub-theme complaints, plus multiple additional mentions in 'Other safety hazard'), oil and coolant caps left unsecured, and bonnets not latched — all post-repair errors that occur after the technical work is done. These are not diagnostic failures; they are process failures preventable by a structured handover check. The sample includes a customer who nearly lost control of a vehicle when a bonnet popped on a highway, another who had a wheel wobble on the freeway, and another whose greasy brake pedal caused their foot to slip. These represent serious liability exposure. A checklist directly addresses the root cause.

actions.action: Implement a 'Safety Fault Verification' protocol requiring that any vehicle booked in for a safety-critical complaint (brakes, steering, suspension, wheels, fluid leaks, bonnet/latches) must undergo a documented, signed road-test or bench-test by the technician AND a second-check by the service advisor before the job is closed. If the original fault cannot be confirmed as resolved, the job must remain open and the customer contacted within 2 business hours with a specific update — not a promise to call back. For repeat-visit safety faults (same fault returning within 30 days), escalate automatically to the Workshop Foreman who must personally inspect and approve the repair. Pilot at VIC07 (Ballarat) and QLD01 (Chermside) — both 9 issues each — to validate the process before group-wide rollout.
actions.owner: Workshop Foreman (verification and escalation), Service Advisor (communication), Service Manager (process compliance)
actions.measure: (1) Reduction in 'same fault returned' safety complaints — the data shows a substantial proportion of brake, steering, suspension, and fluid leak complaints are repeat visits where the original fault was not resolved, including multiple customers on their 2nd, 3rd, or 4th visit for the same issue. Target: fewer than 5% of safety-related jobs result in a same-fault return within 30 days. (2) Track the proportion of safety-critical job cards that include a completed road-test sign-off — target 100%. (3) Customer follow-up call or SMS 48 hours post-collection for all safety-critical repairs, measuring satisfaction with fault resolution — target 85% confirmation the fault is resolved.
actions.rationale: Steering and suspension complaints (33) and brake failure/issues (20) together account for 53 of 131 issues and are dominated by a single pattern: the repair was declared complete but the fault persisted or returned within days. Examples include power steering returning within two days, brake judder unchanged after rotor work, coolant leaks returning within a week, clutch still slipping on hills, and CV joint clicking unchanged after boot replacement. This is a quality-of-diagnosis and quality-of-verification problem — technicians are closing jobs without confirming the fault is resolved. The 'Other safety hazard' category (66 issues, the largest) also contains many cases where the repair was incomplete or introduced a new hazard (burning smell after service, new whining noise post-service, grease on pedals). A mandatory verification step breaks the cycle of repeat visits for unresolved safety faults, which also carries significant legal and reputational risk for the group.

actions.action: Launch a group-wide Safety Recall and Critical Parts Backorder Response Protocol. For any open safety recall, the dealership must contact the customer within 5 business days of the recall notification being issued and offer a booking within 10 weeks maximum — or, if parts are unavailable, provide a written interim safety assessment and a firm parts ETA. For safety-critical parts on backorder (brake pads, wheel nuts, steering components), the service advisor must proactively contact the customer within 24 hours of identifying the backorder, provide a weekly written update (SMS or email), and actively source the part from alternative authorised suppliers or inter-dealership transfer. Customers must not be left to chase updates. A shared parts-availability dashboard across the 24 dealerships should be introduced to enable inter-site sourcing. Additionally, EV customers (a smaller but emerging sub-issue) must receive a standardised EV handover briefing covering charging cable safety, port types, range degradation in cold/highway conditions, and overnight charging behaviour — delivered at point of collection and supported by a one-page printed guide.
actions.owner: Parts Manager (backorder escalation and inter-site sourcing), Service Advisor (customer communication), Sales Manager (EV handover briefing), Group Operations Manager (dashboard implementation)
actions.measure: (1) Zero customers waiting more than 10 weeks for a booked safety recall appointment — track via recall job card open dates. (2) Fewer than 10% of safety-critical backorder cases result in a customer-initiated contact for a status update (i.e., the dealership proactively communicates first). (3) EV-related safety complaints (currently a small but present sub-theme — charging confusion, overheating, range anxiety on highways) tracked separately; target zero EV handover safety complaints within 90 days of briefing rollout. (4) Inter-dealership parts transfers for safety-critical items logged monthly — use as a proxy for whether the shared dashboard is being used.
actions.rationale: This action addresses two distinct but lower-volume patterns that nonetheless carry safety and compliance implications. First, the data contains multiple complaints about safety recalls not being actioned promptly — one customer rang about a recall letter and was never called back, another was told a 10-week wait for a recall booking. Recall non-completion is a regulatory and liability issue that sits outside normal service quality. Second, critical parts unavailability (brake pads, wheel nuts, timing belt kits) is forcing customers to drive vehicles in unsafe or marginal condition for weeks — one customer drove for six weeks with a tail light assembly missing, another with a window sealed with hand-taped plastic, and a fleet operator couldn't plan work around a van with no brake part ETA. The EV sub-theme is noted as a hypothesis given the small sample: comments about charging cable uncertainty, unexpected range loss on the Hume, and overnight charging anxiety suggest a systemic handover gap as EV volumes grow across the dealership group. This action has lower immediate impact than Actions 1 and 2 because it addresses frequency and process rather than the acute post-repair safety failures, but failure to act on recalls in particular carries regulatory risk that management should not defer.

actions.action: Conduct an emergency IT audit of the online booking platform's integration with the workshop management system (DMS), specifically targeting: (a) real-time slot sync failures that allow the site to confirm bookings the DMS never receives, (b) the 8am drop-off double-booking bug explicitly described by multiple customers, (c) session timeout/logout errors that discard bookings before confirmation, and (d) mobile responsiveness failures (date picker non-functional on phones). Following audit, implement a mandatory 'booking lock' mechanism so that a confirmed booking email cannot be generated unless a corresponding job card is simultaneously created in the DMS. Until the fix is verified stable, add a prominent banner on the booking site directing customers to call to confirm, and train front desk staff at VIC01 (Dandenong) and NSW01 (Parramatta) — the two highest-volume affected sites — to proactively cross-check online bookings against the DMS each morning and call any customer whose booking has no matching job card before they travel in.
actions.owner: IT/Digital team (audit and fix); Service Operations Manager (interim front desk protocol); dealership principals at VIC01 and NSW01 (local execution)
actions.measure: (1) 'Booking lost / not recorded' complaints reduce from 56 to fewer than 10 within 90 days of fix deployment. (2) Zero recurrence of confirmed-email-but-no-job-card incidents, measured via weekly DMS reconciliation report. (3) Online booking completion rate (sessions that result in a DMS job card) tracked monthly — target 95%+ within 60 days of fix.
actions.rationale: This is the single most damaging sub-theme: 56 'booking lost / not recorded' complaints plus 47 'online booking system issues' together account for 103 of 217 issues (47%). The comments describe a clear and consistent pattern — customers receive confirmation emails or numbers, arrive, and the workshop has no record. Multiple comments explicitly name the confirmation-email-but-no-DMS-entry failure mode. The 8am double-booking bug is called out by name. IT/Digital is implicated in 55 of the 217 departmental attributions. VIC01 (32) and NSW01 (31) are disproportionately affected and likely share the same platform instance. This is not a training or culture problem — it is a system defect causing real customer harm (lost work days, taken leave, travel with toddlers and elderly relatives) and is the root cause of a significant portion of the trend increase.

actions.action: Implement a proactive rescheduling protocol to eliminate silent cancellations and unnotified slot changes: (a) Any booking change or cancellation must trigger an automated outbound SMS and email to the customer within 30 minutes of the change being made, including the reason (e.g., 'workshop overbooked', 'part unavailable') and a direct callback number — not a generic reception queue. (b) A member of the bookings team must personally call the customer within 2 hours of the automated message if the change is within 48 hours of the appointment. (c) Establish a live cancellation waitlist in the DMS so that customers who cannot be accommodated are offered the next available slot from confirmed cancellations — this directly addresses the multiple complaints of 'put on a cancellation list, never heard back.' (d) Where a rescheduled customer cannot be seen within 7 days, escalate to the Service Manager to source capacity (e.g., extended hours, overflow to a nearby group site). Priority escalation should apply automatically to fleet/commercial customers (referenced by multiple B2B complaints at VIC01 and NSW01) and any safety-critical items such as the one Critical-severity recall complaint in this dataset.
actions.owner: Booking/Scheduling team (protocol and waitlist management); Service Manager (escalation and capacity decisions); dealership principals at VIC01, NSW01, VIC02 for rollout sequencing
actions.measure: (1) 'Booking changed without notice' complaints reduce from 46 to fewer than 10 within 90 days. (2) Measure the proportion of rescheduled customers who receive outbound contact within 2 hours — target 100%. (3) Waitlist conversion rate: percentage of waitlisted customers offered and accepting a slot within 7 days — target 70%+ within 60 days. (4) Monitor fleet account retention by tracking repeat bookings from identified commercial customers at VIC01 and NSW01.
actions.rationale: 'Booking changed without notice' is 46 complaints — the second-largest sub-theme and the one generating the most visceral customer anger in the feedback (all-caps complaints, references to lost income, broken family plans, crew sitting idle, vans off the road). The harm is compounded when customers can't reach a named contact (Raj, Bec, Aroha, Kylie, Mick all named as unreachable after messages left). Importantly, the staff interactions themselves are consistently rated positively — the brand has goodwill to protect. The waitlist failure is a quick operational fix with outsized loyalty impact. The single Critical complaint likely relates to the recall item mentioned ('there's a recall item and I was told they couldn't fit me in for ten weeks'), which represents a compliance and safety risk that should be escalated immediately regardless of this broader action.

actions.action: Commission a capacity and demand analysis across all 24 sites, beginning with VIC01, NSW01, VIC02, NSW02, and QLD03 (Ipswich), to determine whether wait times of 5–11 weeks for standard logbook services reflect a genuine technician capacity shortfall, a scheduling inefficiency (e.g., over-blocking time per job, poor job mix planning), or an online-vs-phone slot visibility mismatch. The data strongly suggests the latter is partly true — multiple customers report the website showing no availability while phone staff can offer immediate slots; this alone is an IT/scheduling configuration fix. Based on findings: (a) If a capacity shortfall is confirmed, present a business case to group management for additional service technician headcount or extended trading hours at the top-5 affected sites. (b) If it is a slot visibility issue, configure the booking platform to surface cancellations and phone-only slots in real time. (c) Regardless of cause, implement a maximum published wait time standard (hypothesis: 2–3 weeks for routine services is a defensible target for a 24-site group) and track compliance monthly. (d) Review whether the current online booking system's service categories (one customer was rejected with 'invalid selection' for choosing 'general service') align with plain-language options accessible to low-automotive-literacy customers, CALD customers, and elderly users — all groups explicitly represented in the complaint data.
actions.owner: Group Service Operations Manager (analysis and business case); IT/Digital (slot visibility fix); HR/Workforce Planning (headcount case if capacity confirmed); individual dealership Service Managers (local execution)
actions.measure: (1) Average days to next available routine service appointment, tracked weekly per site — target under 15 business days at all top-5 sites within 6 months. (2) Eliminate the website-vs-phone availability discrepancy: online and phone slots should match within 30 minutes of any change (verifiable via mystery shop). (3) Online booking abandonment rate (customers who start but don't complete a booking) — target reduction of 30% within 90 days of UX/category fixes. (4) CALD and accessibility complaints within this theme reduce to zero within two review cycles.
actions.rationale: 'No availability / long wait for slot' is the largest sub-theme at 68 complaints, but it is also the least diagnostically clear from the data alone — we cannot confirm whether this is a true capacity problem, a scheduling configuration problem, or a perception problem driven by the broken online system discouraging customers who could have been accommodated by phone. The website-vs-phone discrepancy is evidenced directly in the comments ('website says fully booked, phone says otherwise') and is likely inflating the perceived unavailability figure. This action is Priority 3 not because the issue is less important (long waits for safety-critical items like timing belts and a recall are serious) but because: (a) some of it may be resolved as a by-product of the Priority 1 IT fix, (b) a capacity business case requires data collection before action, and (c) the other two actions will deliver faster, measurable relief. The trend is increasing (H1 to H2), which makes this analysis urgent even if the remediation takes longer.

actions.action: Conduct a network-wide stock rationalisation for high-frequency, high-velocity parts across all 24 dealerships. The National Parts Manager must pull 12 months of job card data to identify the top 200 most-ordered parts per vehicle platform (with particular focus on the Altura Corsa, Altura Vista, Kodiak Ridge, and GT models — repeatedly cited in feedback). Establish mandatory minimum stock levels ('floor stock') for these items at all sites, with priority given to the five highest-complaint dealerships: VIC01 Dandenong, VIC03 Essendon, VIC02 Ringwood, NSW01 Parramatta, and VIC06 Geelong. Implement a cross-dealership stock-sharing protocol so that when a site is out of stock, the system automatically checks other group sites before placing an interstate or overseas order. Feedback repeatedly references absurd stockouts — cabin filters, brake pads, spark plugs, oil filters, headlight globes, bolts — for cars the group itself sells new. This is the most structurally solvable sub-issue and underpins both the 'Part not in stock' (126 issues) and 'Extended back-order / supply delay' (146 issues) categories.
actions.owner: National Parts Manager, supported by Group IT (for stock-sharing system integration) and each site's Parts Manager for local implementation
actions.measure: (1) Reduction in 'Part not in stock' complaints from 126 in current period to below 60 within two reporting cycles. (2) Average parts wait time (measured from job card open to part received) reduced by at least 40% within 6 months. (3) Cross-dealership stock transfers logged monthly — target at least 30% of current interstate orders replaced by intra-group transfers. (4) Floor stock compliance audit score of 90%+ across all 24 sites by end of quarter 1 post-implementation.
actions.rationale: This is the root cause of the majority of complaints. 422 of 299 issues (across both 'not in stock' and 'back-order' sub-themes) stem directly from inadequate stock holdings. The trend is increasing (H1 to H2), suggesting the problem is worsening, not correcting itself. Multiple comments reference routine consumables — brake pads, oil filters, spark plugs, cabin filters — being unavailable at franchise dealerships for cars they sell. Several long-tenure customers (20+ years) specifically note this is a recent deterioration, suggesting a systemic change in ordering policy or supply chain that management should investigate. The five top-affected sites are clustered in metropolitan VIC and western Sydney, where vehicle volumes should make the business case for higher floor stock straightforward. Note: the data does not confirm whether the stockout rate is higher at these sites due to higher throughput volume or poorer ordering discipline — that should be audited before setting floor stock targets.

actions.action: Implement a mandatory automated parts status communication workflow across all dealerships. Using the existing DMS (Dealer Management System), configure automated outbound SMS and/or email touchpoints triggered at: (1) point of parts order placement — customer notified that a part has been ordered, with supplier ETA included; (2) any change to ETA — automatic notification sent within 2 hours of the Parts team receiving updated information from the supplier; (3) part arrival confirmation — SMS sent same day the part is booked in, with a prompt to schedule the fitment appointment. Where automation is not yet technically feasible at a site, mandate a manual call/SMS process with same-day compliance, logged in the DMS job card. Parts Managers at all sites must run a daily open-order report each morning and ensure every line item with an outstanding ETA has had customer contact within the previous 48 hours. This directly addresses the 'No communication about part status' sub-theme (27 explicit complaints), but the actual scale is likely much larger — dozens of comments describe customers who only discovered part status by repeatedly calling in or physically visiting the dealership.
actions.owner: Group Customer Experience Manager (policy and DMS configuration), Parts Managers at each site (daily compliance), Group IT (automation build)
actions.measure: (1) 'No communication about part status' complaints reduced from 27 to under 5 per reporting period within two cycles. (2) DMS audit: 95%+ of open parts orders must have a logged customer contact event within 48 hours of any status change. (3) Customer satisfaction score (CSI or equivalent) for 'kept informed during wait' metric to reach 75%+ positive within 6 months. (4) Track inbound 'where is my part?' calls to Parts desk — target 50% reduction within 3 months of go-live as a proxy for proactive communication effectiveness.
actions.measure_note: The 27 explicit complaints almost certainly undercount the true scale of this issue — the majority of delay complaints also describe customers who had to self-initiate every update. Treat 27 as a floor, not a ceiling.
actions.rationale: The 'No communication' sub-theme generated only 27 explicit complaints, but it is a compounding factor in the vast majority of the 146 back-order and 126 out-of-stock complaints. Comments include customers who discovered a part had been sitting ready for a week with no notification, customers who rang multiple times and were promised callbacks that never came, and customers who only found out a part was unavailable on the day of drop-off — having taken time off work. This is also relatively low-cost to address compared to stock rationalisation, and a quick win that can improve sentiment even while structural stock issues are resolved. A small number of comments (e.g., 'Honestly the texts were the best bit') suggest that where proactive communication does exist it is well-received — this should be investigated as a potential internal best-practice model to scale.

actions.action: Introduce a Parts Delay Escalation and Alternative Sourcing Protocol. When a part has been on back-order for more than 5 business days with no confirmed ETA, the Parts Manager must formally escalate via a defined process: (1) check all other group dealerships for available stock; (2) check approved aftermarket suppliers (e.g., Gates, Bosch, Ryco equivalents) for a compliant alternative — customer must be offered this option with transparent pricing; (3) where the vehicle is off-road and the customer is experiencing hardship (work vehicle, sole transport, family with children), trigger a loan car assessment by the Service Manager. This protocol should be documented, trained, and compliance-checked via monthly job card audits. Parts counter staff should be empowered and scripted to proactively offer alternatives rather than defaulting to 'we only use what we order' (directly quoted in feedback). For nationally back-ordered items, Parts Managers should be required to check national distributor alternatives and document why an alternative was or was not used.
actions.owner: Group Service Operations Manager (protocol design and training), Parts Managers (daily execution), Service Managers (loan car decisions)
actions.measure: (1) Average resolution time for parts orders exceeding 5 business days — target reduction of 30% within 2 quarters. (2) Number of alternative-source resolutions logged per month (currently likely near zero based on feedback — baseline to be established in month 1). (3) High-severity parts complaints (currently 95 'High' + 2 'Critical') — target reduction to below 50 High and 0 Critical within two reporting periods. (4) Spot-check audit of job cards for back-orders older than 5 days: 100% should have a documented escalation action.
actions.rationale: Multiple comments reference situations where the customer themselves identified an alternative source (online, aftermarket, other dealership in the group) that staff either hadn't considered or refused to explore. The cam belt kit comment ('I told Gaz the OEM kit is common and Gates do it same-day — blank stare') and the EGR valve comment ('I found the same part online from a local supplier in two minutes') are illustrative. With 95 High-severity and 2 Critical complaints in this theme, there are real cases involving vehicles off the road for extended periods with significant financial and personal impact — particularly tradespeople, families, and financially vulnerable customers (students, pensioners) mentioned repeatedly in the feedback. This action is ranked third because it is dependent on staff training and cultural change, which takes longer to embed than the stock and communication fixes above. However, it addresses the tail-end worst cases and should reduce the High/Critical severity cluster meaningfully.

actions.action: Implement a mandatory, structured EV handover checklist for all Voltra Arc and Voltra E3 deliveries, covering: (1) home charging setup including wall socket compatibility and wallbox requirements, (2) charge port flap release (manual and app), (3) slow vs fast charge port difference, (4) range display interpretation including impact of weather, speed, and towing, (5) connected app setup completed in-person before customer leaves the lot, and (6) public charger operation walkthrough. The checklist must be co-signed by the delivering salesperson and customer, scanned to the DMS, and handover must be blocked from closure without a completed form. Minimum handover time of 30 minutes to be enforced by Sales Managers. Focus immediate rollout on QLD01 (Chermside, 17 issues), NSW03 (Chatswood, 16 issues), QLD04 (Southport, 12 issues), and VIC05 (Box Hill, 12 issues).
actions.owner: Sales Department — General Managers at each affected site, overseen by Group Sales Director
actions.measure: Post-handover survey (sent via SMS 48 hours after delivery) question: 'Were you shown how to charge your EV and use the app before leaving the dealership?' Target: 90% positive response within 90 days. Secondary measure: reduction in EV-related 'Vehicle Knowledge' complaints from current ~60% of all theme issues to below 20% within two review cycles. DMS compliance audit: 100% of EV deliveries to have signed checklist on file.
actions.rationale: EV charging and app knowledge is overwhelmingly the dominant sub-issue — conservatively 55–65 of the 85 'Poor/no explanation' complaints reference charging cable use, range display confusion, app setup, charge port operation, or home charging compatibility. This is not a hypothesis; the pattern is explicit and repeated across Sales (51 issues) and Service (34 issues) touchpoints, and spans all five top-affected sites. Customers are being handed sealed cable bags, told 'good luck,' and left to YouTube basics in carparks. Several comments reference near-dangerous outcomes (stranded at chargers, nearly running flat on the Hume). The trend is increasing (H1 to H2), suggesting EV volume is growing faster than staff capability or process. This single action addresses the largest, most urgent cluster of harm.

actions.action: Design and deliver a mandatory product knowledge certification program for all customer-facing Sales and Service Advisors across the group, with three tiers: (Tier 1) ICE/hybrid vehicle features, technology, and service explanation — all staff; (Tier 2) EV-specific technical knowledge including charging infrastructure, range factors, and app ecosystems — all EV-selling and EV-servicing staff; (Tier 3) plain-language communication skills for explaining technical content to low-literacy, CALD, elderly, and first-time buyer customers — all staff. Training to be delivered by OEM product trainers supplemented by in-house role-play sessions. Certification must be completed before staff are permitted to conduct solo handovers or advise on service invoices. Recertification required every 12 months or upon introduction of a new model. Staff who receive two or more attributed knowledge complaints within a quarter to be placed on a targeted coaching plan by their direct manager.
actions.owner: People & Culture / Training Manager (group level), with Site Principals accountable for completion rates at their dealership
actions.measure: (1) 100% of customer-facing Sales and Service staff certified within 60 days of program launch. (2) Post-interaction survey score for 'Staff explained things clearly in a way I understood' — target average of 4.2/5.0 or above within 120 days. (3) Volume of 'Poor/no explanation' sub-theme complaints (currently 85 of 91 issues) to reduce by at least 40% in the following half-year period. (4) Zero repeat attributions of dismissive or condescending behaviour (eye-rolling, 'I already told you,' jargon dismissal) — tracked via complaint tagging in CRM.
actions.rationale: Beyond EV-specific gaps, the data reveals a systemic failure to explain anything clearly — warranty, service schedules, logbook meaning, invoice line items, drive modes, infotainment, and basic features like opening a petrol cap. Multiple comments reference staff dismissiveness toward customers who self-identified as inexperienced ('spoke to me like I was stupid,' 'rolled his eyes,' 'I already told you'). This affects both Sales (51 issues) and Service (34 issues), indicating the problem is cultural and capability-based, not process-based alone. CALD customers and elderly customers appear particularly underserved based on comment patterns — this is a hypothesis given the sample, but a credible one given the frequency and specificity of those references. The checklist in Action 1 fixes the process; this action fixes the people behind it.

actions.action: Develop and distribute a branded, plain-language 'Your EV Ownership Guide' — a two-sided laminated quick-reference card placed in every EV glovebox at delivery, supplemented by a QR code linking to a short-form video series (3–5 minutes each) covering: home charging setup, public charger use, range display explained, charge port manual release, and app walkthrough. Videos to be recorded in English with subtitles, and where site demographics support it, in Mandarin and Vietnamese. The same QR code to be printed on Service invoices for EV customers, linking to a 'What was done to your car today' explainer for common service items. This resource does not replace the in-person handover (Action 1) but acts as a safety net for customers who feel too rushed, shy, or overwhelmed to ask questions in-store.
actions.owner: Marketing Department (content production and translation), with Product/Brand Managers reviewing accuracy; Service Managers to approve invoice QR code integration
actions.measure: (1) QR code scan rate — target minimum 30% of EV deliveries within 7 days of handover, tracked via UTM parameters. (2) Reduction in repeat contact (calls/emails) to dealerships about EV charging basics — Service and Sales reception teams to log 'how do I charge' inbound contacts; target 25% reduction within 90 days of guide distribution. (3) Customer survey item: 'Did you feel you had access to helpful resources after your purchase/service?' — baseline to be established at launch, target 75% positive within 6 months.
actions.rationale: A consistent pattern across comments is customers who felt too rushed, shy, or overwhelmed to ask questions at the time ('I just nodded,' 'I'm a bit shy about asking,' 'my grandson had to do it') and then struggled alone at home. Several reference Googling in carparks or reading manuals with their glasses on. This self-service resource addresses the gap that exists even when staff do a reasonable job but customers don't retain everything. It is ranked third because it is a support mechanism, not a root-cause fix — the checklist and training must come first. Note: the one positive comment in the sub-theme data ('Features/technology explained well') is a signal that when explanation does happen, customers value it highly; this resource extends that value beyond the showroom floor.

actions.action: Implement a mandatory Finance & Insurance (F&I) Consent Protocol across all 24 dealerships: Finance Managers must record a customer's first verbal decline of any add-on product (extended warranty, paint protection, gap insurance, credit life cover, etc.) on a standardised digital form, after which that product cannot be re-raised in the same session. Introduce a post-F&I SMS survey sent within 1 hour of the finance office visit asking one question: 'Did you feel pressured to accept any finance or insurance products today?' (Yes/No). Flag any 'Yes' responses to the State Sales Manager within 24 hours for follow-up. Retrain all Finance Managers and Sales staff on compliant selling practices, with specific focus on recognising and respecting a clear 'no' — referencing actual examples from this feedback (students on fixed budgets, retirees, customers with pre-arranged finance, fleet buyers).
actions.owner: National Finance & Insurance Manager, supported by State Sales Managers at NSW04 (Liverpool), NSW01 (Parramatta), NSW02 (Penrith), QLD01 (Chermside), QLD04 (Southport)
actions.measure: Target: post-F&I 'pressured' SMS response rate below 5% within 90 days; zero repeat-decline violations per Finance Manager per month as evidenced by consent logs; reduction in 'Pressure selling' sub-theme complaints from 47 to under 15 within two review cycles. Also monitor ASIC/AFCA complaints as a lagging indicator.
actions.rationale: Pressure selling is the single largest sub-theme at 47 incidents and accounts for the majority of High severity ratings (59 total). The feedback is unambiguous and repeated: customers are declining products clearly and being ignored — sometimes multiple times in a single session. Comments reference vulnerable customers (pensioners, students, non-English speakers, first-time buyers) being targeted with fast-talking or scare-tactic pitches. This is a compliance risk as well as a CX risk — some behaviours described (implying price changes if finance isn't taken, suggesting a car is 'unsafe' without add-ons) may breach ASIC's responsible lending and unfair conduct obligations. Named staff (Bec, Kylie, Raj, Aroha) appear across multiple comments, suggesting this is systemic rather than isolated. The trend is increasing (H1 to H2), making this the highest-urgency action.

actions.action: Introduce a standardised Pre-Delivery Checklist (PDC) that must be completed and signed off by a Service/PDI Technician AND countersigned by the delivering Sales Consultant before any vehicle is handed to a customer. The checklist must cover: all contracted accessories fitted and verified (floor mats, roof racks, tow bars, tyre pressure monitors, dash cams, tints, number plates, protective film removed, wheel lock keys, spare keys, service books, logbooks, fuel level, tyre inflation, EV charging cables opened and explained, wall-box requirements communicated for EVs). A photo of the completed checklist must be uploaded to the DMS against the deal record. If any item is missing, the handover must be rescheduled — handing over a vehicle with outstanding items requires written customer consent and a committed completion date within 5 business days. Fleet purchases (referencing the 8-vehicle and 5-vehicle incidents) require a dedicated Fleet PDI Coordinator sign-off.
actions.owner: Service/PDI Manager (each dealership), with compliance oversight from the State Operations Manager. NSW04 (Liverpool) and QLD01 (Chermside) to pilot in week 1 given highest complaint volumes.
actions.measure: 'Incomplete handover / missing items' sub-theme complaints (currently 51, the largest sub-theme) to fall by at least 60% within one quarter. PDC completion rate to reach 100% within 30 days of rollout, audited via DMS records. Track re-attendance rate (customers returning to collect missing items) as a secondary KPI — target below 2% of deliveries.
actions.rationale: Incomplete handover is the largest sub-theme at 51 incidents, with a striking pattern of missing items that should have been caught by a pre-delivery inspection: floor mats, roof racks, spare keys, tow bars, wheel lock keys, fuel, plates, protective film, charging cables, and accessories paid for at point of sale. Multiple comments reference the delivery inspection sheet being blank, suggesting the PDI process is either not happening or not being enforced. EV-specific handover failures (charging cable not explained, wall-box requirement not communicated, drive modes not demonstrated) are a growing subset and a reputational risk as the EV mix increases. Fleet complaints (missing items across multiple vehicles, inconsistent admin charges) suggest the standard PDC, if it exists, is not being applied to fleet deals. This is largely a process and accountability gap — a well-enforced checklist is a high-confidence fix.

actions.action: Design and deliver a structured Vehicle Handover Experience (VHE) standard: every customer receives a minimum 30-minute handover appointment (60 minutes for EV or fleet), booked in the DMS as a distinct diary event separate from the sales consultant's availability. The handover must include: a walkaround of the vehicle (exterior condition, accessories confirmed), a cabin orientation (key features, infotainment pairing, drive modes, EV charging setup where applicable), confirmation of all documents (contract, logbook, service book, spare key), and a 'first drive' offer where the consultant or product specialist sits with the customer for 5 minutes. Handovers cannot be conducted in the last 30 minutes of the business day without State Manager approval. A 48-hour post-handover SMS must be sent asking: 'On a scale of 1–5, how confident do you feel using your new vehicle?' with a free-text follow-up for scores of 1–3.
actions.owner: Sales Manager (each dealership) responsible for scheduling; Product Specialists or Senior Sales Consultants to conduct handovers. Training to be developed by the National Customer Experience team.
actions.measure: Post-handover confidence SMS average score above 4.0 within 60 days of rollout. 'Rushed handover' mentions (currently embedded across ~20+ comments in the incomplete handover sub-theme) to fall below 5 per quarter. Zero handovers conducted in the last 30 minutes of day without approval, audited via DMS timestamps.
actions.rationale: Rushed handovers are consistently described across the feedback — durations of '5 minutes', '10 minutes', '15 minutes tops' — with customers leaving unable to operate basic vehicle features, find reverse, open the fuel cap, or understand EV charging. This is distinct from missing items (Action 2) and is instead a time and process problem: handovers are being squeezed around sales consultant schedules, closing time pressures (two explicit references to 'ten to five' and 'he had to leave'), or the next customer. Several comments note the irony that the finance office spent 40 minutes pushing add-ons while the actual vehicle handover lasted five minutes. This action is ranked third because it requires scheduling and training change rather than a compliance intervention, and the impact — while real — is less acute than pressure selling or missing items. However, for EV customers and first-time buyers (both explicitly mentioned as underserved), this represents a significant loyalty and safety risk that will compound as EV volumes grow.

actions.action: Implement a mandatory twice-daily facilities inspection checklist (7:30am and 12:30pm) across all 24 dealerships, covering toilets (soap, paper towel, cleanliness, locks, change tables), waiting area (tables wiped, bins emptied, cups cleared, floor clean), coffee machine status, and car park condition. Inspection sign-off must be completed by a named Site Coordinator and logged in a shared digital system (e.g., a simple Google Form or facilities management app) visible to the State Facilities Manager. Any item marked as defective must be escalated and resolved within 2 hours or a customer-facing 'out of service' notice with an ETA must be posted. Prioritise VIC06 (Geelong), QLD02 (Springwood), and VIC03 (Essendon) for immediate rollout given they account for 36 of the top 54 complaints across the five worst sites.
actions.owner: Facilities/Site Management — Site Coordinators at each dealership, overseen by State Facilities Managers (VIC, QLD, NSW)
actions.measure: Reduction in Facilities & Amenities complaints from current 127 per period to below 60 within two quarters; cleanliness sub-theme (currently the highest at 36 issues) and toilets (21 issues) to drop by at least 50%; digital inspection logs to show 95%+ completion rate within 60 days of rollout; coffee machine 'out of order' complaints (appearing in at least 10 sampled comments) to fall to near zero
actions.rationale: Cleanliness (36), toilets (21), and refreshments (18) together account for 59% of all sub-theme complaints and are overwhelmingly driven by basic maintenance failures — overflowing bins, dirty floors, no soap, no paper towel, broken locks, and a coffee machine that multiple customers report has displayed an 'out of order' sign across consecutive visits. These are not capital expenditure problems; they are process and accountability gaps. The trend is increasing (H1 to H2), meaning inaction is compounding the problem.
